episode.observableAction: Late morning light comes in through the small front-room window of the flat. The subject and the older sibling sit on the worn rug with a single red plastic truck between them. The sibling rolls the truck in a wide circle, making engine noises, while the subject reaches for it and says they want to build a line of blocks for the truck to drive through. The sibling pulls the truck back and says they are using it to race. The subject picks up a wooden block and sets it upright in front of the truck’s path. The sibling pushes the truck forward anyway, knocking the block over, and says that knocking things down is part of the race. The subject moves two more blocks into a narrow gate shape and holds them steady with both hands. The sibling stops the truck just short of the blocks and says that if they are going to make a gate, the truck has to go fast through it. The subject says the truck has to stop at the gate first. The two of them go back and forth, repeating “fast” and “stop” while tapping the truck and the blocks. After a pause, the sibling suggests counting to three before pushing the truck. The subject nods and moves the blocks slightly wider apart. The sibling holds the truck at the edge of the rug, counts “one, two, three” out loud, and then pushes it so it rolls through the widened gate without hitting the blocks. Both children watch the truck pass through and then reset the blocks and truck to do it again.

episode.observableAction: On a cool mid-morning in the small front room, the subject and older sibling sit on the rug with the same red plastic truck and a shallow cardboard box lid. The sibling places the box lid upside down on a stack of two books to make a low ramp and pushes the truck so it rolls up and bumps off the edge. The subject shakes their head, moves one book away to lower the ramp, and says the truck should fly farther. The sibling replaces the truck at the bottom, pushes harder and watches it rattle up and drop only a short distance from the books. The subject then slides the remaining book back to steepen the ramp again and taps the floor farther away, saying the truck should land there. The sibling frowns, lifts the box lid to flatten it almost level and says that is the right way, then sets the truck and nudges it so it barely rolls off the edge and stops close to the stack. The subject reaches for the book under the ramp, the sibling keeps a hand on the box lid and says they are using it, and the two pause with hands on opposite sides of the ramp until the subject lets go of the book and instead pulls the truck back to the start of the ramp. The sibling releases the box lid, shifts it to rest on one book again, and says they will both push from the same place. They line the truck’s front wheels with a crack in the rug, count together to three, and take turns pushing the truck up the ramp from that mark, watching where it lands and then dragging it back to the crack to do it again.

episode.observableAction: On a late afternoon in the small front room, the subject and older sibling kneel on the rug with the red plastic truck and a shallow cardboard box lid, arguing over whether the truck should jump from the lid onto a cushion or crash into a stack of books; the subject pushes the truck up the tilted lid toward the cushion while saying it has to land softly, the sibling pulls the truck back and shoves the books closer, saying it has to hit them, and they each keep a hand on the truck, tugging it in opposite directions until a wheel pops off and rolls under the low table. Both children freeze and look toward the kitchen doorway, where a caregiver, drying their hands on a towel, steps in, bends to pick up the loose wheel, and without asking takes the truck from the children, snaps the wheel back into place with a firm push, tests the wheels by rolling the truck once across the rug, and then sets it down between the subject and sibling before turning back toward the kitchen.

On a gray late afternoon in the small front room, the subject and older sibling sit at the low table with a sheet of lined paper between them, taking turns writing short sums in pencil while a school notebook lies open to a page of similar problems; the subject slowly copies “7 + 5 =” from the notebook and hesitates with the pencil above the blank, the sibling leans over and whispers a different number than the one printed in the notebook’s answer column, and the subject writes that whispered number on the paper. Before they move to the next line, a caregiver comes in from the kitchen drying their hands on a dish towel, glances down at the page, and without asking picks up the pencil, crosses out the subject’s answer with a single firm line, writes the printed answer from the notebook beside it, taps the corrected sum twice with the pencil tip, and then sets the pencil back on the table and returns toward the kitchen while the two children look at the altered line.

On a quiet mid-afternoon in the municipal reading room, the subject walks slowly along a low shelf of mixed paperbacks and thin hardbacks, tilting their head to read the spines while a few adults sit scattered at nearby tables with newspapers. The subject pauses, pulls out a slim book with a bright cover showing a ferry against a gray sky, glances at the covers of two other books on the same shelf, then returns one and keeps the ferry book in hand. They carry it to an empty table, place it flat, and open it near the middle, running a finger briefly under a line of printed text before turning the book back to the first page and settling their elbows on the table to read from the top while the room’s wall clock ticks and a chair scrapes softly in the background.

episode.observableAction: Late on a Sunday morning, the subject and older sibling sit on the floor of the small flat near a low table, with a single box of colored pencils between them and a few sheets of paper spread out. The subject pulls the box closer and begins lining the pencils up in a row by length, while the sibling reaches over, takes several from the row, and starts shading in a large drawing on their own page. The subject slides the box back toward them and gathers the scattered pencils, saying that they still need the blue one for their picture. The sibling keeps coloring with the blue pencil and says they need it to finish the sky. The two children go back and forth, each keeping a hand on the box, until the sibling suggests that they use the blue pencil in turns, counting to ten each time before passing it. The subject hesitates, then lets go of the box. The sibling counts aloud to ten while coloring, then places the blue pencil in the middle of the table. The subject picks it up, colors quickly on their own page while counting to ten, and then sets it back in the middle. They continue alternating this way, both leaning over their papers and reaching for the shared pencil when it is their turn.

episode.observableAction: On a cool Saturday morning in the small flat, the subject and older sibling sit at the low table with a single worn board game spread out, each moving pieces along a track drawn on the cardboard; when the subject rolls the dice and moves a piece past the finish square, the sibling objects and says they have to land exactly on the finish, while the subject insists that passing it still counts as winning. Their voices rise as they repeat their positions and gesture at the printed finish line until a caregiver, passing through with a mug of tea, pauses beside the table, asks, "How did you say the rule at the start?" and listens while each child explains their version, then suggests they restart the game after agreeing together whether the piece must land exactly on the finish or can go past it, leaving them to decide before walking back toward the kitchen.

On a late afternoon in the small flat, the subject and older sibling sit on the floor near the low table with a single rubber ball between them, agreeing to play a game where the ball must bounce once on the table before being caught. After a few turns, the subject throws the ball so it hits the table edge and skims off the side; the sibling catches it and says that throw does not count because it did not land flat on the tabletop, while the subject insists it still bounced on the table. They pause the game, each pointing at the table surface and edge, repeating their versions of the rule and demonstrating different throws toward the tabletop and the edge, until they agree aloud that from then on the ball has to touch the flat top, not just the side, before they resume taking turns.

episode.observableAction: On a grey Sunday afternoon in the small flat, the subject sits cross-legged on the floor by the low table with an open school notebook and a half-finished colored drawing of a ferry and water, several colored pencils scattered around. The older sibling is nearby on the sofa flipping through a comic. A caregiver comes in from the kitchen drying their hands on a towel, pauses behind the subject, leans over to look at the page and says, "Oh, you’re drawing the ferry again," then taps the blue area and adds, "I like how you made the water darker under the boat," before straightening up and walking toward the hallway. The sibling glances over, shifts off the sofa to kneel beside the table, picks up a green pencil and traces a short line in the corner of their own scrap paper while looking at the subject’s drawing.

On a quiet Sunday afternoon in the municipal reading room, the subject walks slowly along a low shelf of children’s and youth books, tilting their head to read the spines while other visitors sit at nearby tables with newspapers. The subject pauses, pulls out a thin paperback with a bright cover showing a ferry on choppy water, flips it over to glance at the back, then slides it back halfway before stopping, taking it out again and opening to the middle. After looking at a page with a simple diagram of a boat and arrows pointing to labeled parts, the subject closes the book, tucks it under one arm, and carries it to the front desk, where an unseen adult hand reaches out from behind the counter to scan it and place a stamped borrowing slip inside before the subject turns away holding the book against their chest and walks toward the exit.

Late morning light comes in through the small living-room window of the flat. The subject and the older sibling sit on the worn rug with a shallow cardboard box between them, sorting a mixed pile of colored pencils and short crayons. The sibling pushes the box closer and says they should put all the long pencils on one side and the small broken pieces on the other. The subject reaches for a stubby blue pencil and says it should go with the long ones because it still has a point. The sibling shakes their head and moves the blue stub toward the short side of the box. The subject pulls it back and says they want to use it for drawing. The sibling says they need the box to close properly and starts lining the long pencils flat along one edge. The subject holds the blue stub in their fist and keeps the lid from coming down. The two of them pause, then the sibling suggests putting the blue stub in the corner so the lid can still shut. The subject looks at the corner space, places the blue stub there, and lets go of the lid. The sibling closes the box carefully, checking that it stays shut, while the subject watches and then picks the box up to shake it lightly.

Late afternoon light falls across the small kitchen table in the flat. The subject and the older sibling sit opposite each other with a single lined notebook open between them and one short pencil on the table. The sibling has drawn a large circle and says it is their turn to make a game board. The subject reaches for the pencil and says they want to draw the paths. The sibling pulls the notebook slightly toward themselves and says they are still using it. The subject tugs the top corner of the page back and the notebook shifts, bumping against a cup. The pencil rolls toward the edge of the table and drops to the floor. Both children slide off their chairs at the same time and reach under the table, bumping shoulders as they grab for the pencil. The subject closes their hand around it first and stands up, holding it against their chest. The sibling stands too and says they need it to finish the circle. The subject shakes their head and keeps their fist closed around the pencil. Footsteps sound in the hallway and caregiver 1 appears in the doorway, wiping their hands on a dish towel. They look at the two children, step closer, and gently take the notebook from the table. Without asking either child, caregiver 1 walks to the low shelf by the window, opens a drawer, and takes out another stubby pencil. They place the second pencil on the table next to the notebook, slide the notebook back to the middle, and say that now each of them has one. The subject slowly opens their hand and looks at the pencil they are holding, while the sibling picks up the new pencil and leans over the notebook to continue drawing the circle.

episode.observableAction: Early evening light comes through the living-room window of the flat. The subject and the older sibling sit on the floor near the low table with a single battered school ruler between them, using it to draw straight lines on separate sheets of paper. The sibling pulls the ruler toward their side and says they need it to finish the border on their page. The subject reaches across, says it is their turn, and tugs the ruler back so that both of them are holding it and the papers slide crooked on the table. The sibling pulls harder, the ruler twists, and one end knocks over a plastic cup of water, spilling it across both drawings. The subject lets go of the ruler and grabs their paper, lifting the dripping sheet with both hands, while the sibling lifts theirs and complains that the lines are ruined. Caregiver 2 comes in from the kitchen, takes the wet papers from each child, lays them flat on a dry section of the table, and uses a dish towel to blot the water from the table and the edges of the pages. Without asking either child, caregiver 2 picks up the ruler, places it in the middle of the table, and says they will draw the straight borders for both pages. The caregiver holds the ruler steady, draws a neat rectangle on the sibling’s page, then slides the ruler to the subject’s page and draws another rectangle while the children stand on either side watching.

episode.observableAction: On a cloudy afternoon in the municipal school yard, the subject stands near a low wall watching a group of classmates kick a worn football. The older sibling, who shares the same yard during overlapping break, walks over with two friends and calls out a quick phrase that makes the friends laugh. The subject looks at the sibling and asks what that word means. One friend repeats the phrase more loudly, adds an exaggerated gesture, and the small group laughs again. The subject glances from face to face without joining in, then the bell rings and the sibling shrugs, turns away with the friends, and they all head toward their classroom line while the subject moves to join a different line of students.
